blocks.content: A running program keeps its data in a shape built for speed: objects linked by pointers, scattered across the heap, meaningful only inside that one process, in that one moment. The instant you need to send that data anywhere else, across a network, into a file, into another process entirely, that shape stops being useful. You first have to flatten it into something portable, and then rebuild it faithfully on the other side.

That flattening is serialization. The rebuilding is deserialization. Between the two of them sits the wire, or the disk, or whatever boundary the data has to cross. Nearly every request your server receives and every response it sends passes through both, whether or not you ever think about it directly.

It helps to picture packing furniture for a move. Serialization is disassembling a couch into flat panels that fit through a doorway and into a truck. Deserialization is putting it back together at the other end, following the same instructions in reverse. If a step loses a screw or mislabels a panel along the way, the couch you end up with is not quite the couch you started with, and that gap between what you sent and what arrived is exactly where most of the interesting problems in this topic live.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530153-313013609.png
blocks.alt: Serialization flattens an in-memory object into bytes that can cross the wire, deserialization rebuilds it at the other end

blocks.content: 1. What Serialization and Deserialization Actually Mean
blocks.text: 1. What Serialization and Deserialization Actually Mean

blocks.content: Serialization is the process of converting an in memory data structure, such as an object or a struct, into a format that can be stored on disk or transmitted over a network, usually a sequence of bytes or a text string. Deserialization is the exact reverse: taking that stored or transmitted form and reconstructing the original data structure, ideally with nothing lost along the way.

The two are always discussed as a pair, because one is meaningless without the other. Serializing data you never plan to read back is pointless, and deserializing a format nothing ever produced is impossible. Every system that does one, somewhere, does the other.

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: Serialization turns an object into bytes you can send or save. Deserialization turns those bytes back into an object your code can use.

blocks.title: Marshalling and unmarshalling
blocks.content: Some ecosystems, especially Go and older enterprise Java code, use the terms marshal and unmarshal for exactly this same pair of operations. Different vocabulary, identical idea.

You have almost certainly written both operations without naming them. Calling JSON.stringify(user) serializes a JavaScript object into a JSON string. Calling JSON.parse(body) on the other side deserializes that string back into an object.

A good serializer aims for round trip fidelity: serialize an object, deserialize the result, and you should get back something equal to what you started with in every way that matters to your application. Losing a field, silently changing a type, or reordering data during that round trip is a bug, even when the bytes produced along the way were perfectly valid for the format.

blocks.title: A quick habit worth building
blocks.content: Write a small test that serializes a representative object, immediately deserializes the result, and asserts equality with the original. It catches mapping and type problems while they are cheap to fix, long before they reach production traffic.
2. Why We Need Them At All
blocks.text: 2. Why We Need Them At All

blocks.content: An object living in memory is really just a region of the heap plus a web of pointers, and both of those things are specific to one running process. A pointer that means something inside your Node.js process means nothing to a different process, on a different machine, written in a different language. Before data can leave the process it was created in, it has to be converted into a form that does not depend on any of that internal, process specific structure.

["Network transfer: sending a request body to a server, or a response back to a client, over HTTP or any other protocol.","Storage: writing application state to a file or a database so it survives after the process exits.","Caching: storing a computed object in something like Redis, which only understands bytes and strings, not live objects.","Inter process communication: two processes on the same machine exchanging data through a pipe, a socket, or shared memory.","Cross language communication: letting a Java service and a Python service agree on data without sharing any internal types at all."]
items: Network transfer: sending a request body to a server, or a response back to a client, over HTTP or any other protocol.
Storage: writing application state to a file or a database so it survives after the process exits.
Caching: storing a computed object in something like Redis, which only understands bytes and strings, not live objects.
Inter process communication: two processes on the same machine exchanging data through a pipe, a socket, or shared memory.
Cross language communication: letting a Java service and a Python service agree on data without sharing any internal types at all.

blocks.content: Each of these is really the same underlying problem wearing a different hat: something outside the current process needs the data, and the current process internal representation cannot cross that boundary on its own. Serialization is the universal answer, which is exactly why it shows up in so many unrelated sounding parts of a system.

{"headers":["Need","Concrete Example"],"rows":[["Network transfer","A mobile app sending a JSON request body to a REST API"],["Storage","Writing an application configuration object out to a file on disk"],["Caching","Storing a computed product listing in Redis as a byte string"],["Inter process communication","Two microservices exchanging a Protobuf message over gRPC"]]}

Even two processes running the exact same code on the exact same machine cannot casually hand a live object to one another, because the operating system deliberately gives each process its own private memory space. The instant a value needs to cross that boundary, serialization stops being optional and becomes the only way through.
3. Where This Sits in the Request Pipeline
blocks.text: 3. Where This Sits in the Request Pipeline

blocks.content: By the time deserialization happens, a request has usually already been through routing, the stage covered in the previous topic in this series, which matched the incoming method and path to a specific handler. Routing never looks inside the request body. It only cares about the method and the URL. Once a handler has been selected, the raw body, still just a stream of bytes, has to be turned into something the handler can actually work with, and that conversion is deserialization.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530154-194036287.png
blocks.alt: Deserialization happens right after routing, driven by the Content-Type header, before any validation occurs

blocks.content: In practice this step is usually handled by a body parsing middleware that reads the Content-Type header on the request, for example application/json or application/x-protobuf, and picks the matching deserializer automatically. By the time your handler function runs, req.body is already a plain object, not a string of raw bytes.

What deserialization deliberately does not do is check whether that object is correct. A deserializer will happily produce an object with a negative age or a missing required field, as long as the bytes were structurally valid. Deciding whether the resulting object is actually acceptable is the job of the very next stage, Request Validation and Transformation, which assumes deserialization has already handed it a usable object to inspect.

This ordering is not arbitrary. Validation logic that checks field types and business rules only makes sense once the raw bytes have already become a structured object with named fields. Trying to validate before deserializing would mean writing validation rules against raw text or binary, which nobody actually does in practice.
4. The Mechanics: Encoding and Decoding

Underneath the single word serialization, two distinct steps are actually happening. The first is mapping your data structure onto a format specific representation, deciding how a field named createdAt becomes a key in a JSON object, or a numbered field in a Protobuf message. The second is encoding that representation into actual bytes, for example turning JSON text into a UTF-8 byte sequence, or packing a Protobuf message into its compact binary layout.

Deserialization reverses both steps, but in the opposite order. First comes decoding, turning raw bytes back into the format specific representation, and then comes binding, mapping that representation onto the fields of a target type in your programming language. Both directions have to agree on the same rules, or the round trip breaks.

{"headers":["Direction","Step 1","Step 2"],"rows":[["Serialize","Map object fields to a format representation","Encode that representation into bytes"],["Deserialize","Decode bytes back into a format representation","Bind that representation onto a target type"]]}

blocks.title: Encoding is not the same as encryption
blocks.content: Encoding a payload as UTF-8 bytes or Base64 text makes it transmittable, not secret. Anyone who receives the bytes can decode them just as easily as your own server can. Serialization on its own provides no confidentiality at all.

blocks.title: From object to bytes
blocks.text: The number 65 inside a JSON payload is text: the two ASCII bytes spelling the characters "6" and "5". The same value inside a compact binary format like Protobuf might be a single byte. Same value, two completely different byte layouts, which is exactly why a JSON parser cannot read a Protobuf message, or the reverse.

blocks.content: Serialization is a promise between two sides: they may run different code, in different languages, on different machines, but if they agree on the same bytes, they agree on the same data.
5. Schema Binding and Type Coercion Pitfalls
blocks.text: 5. Schema Binding and Type Coercion Pitfalls

blocks.content: The binding step, matching decoded fields onto a target type, is where a surprising number of real bugs live. JSON, in particular, has a much looser type system than most programming languages, and every gap between what JSON can express and what your language expects is a place data can quietly get mangled.

["Large integers: JSON numbers are represented as floating point, so integers beyond about 2^53 can lose precision silently during a round trip.","Dates: JSON has no native date type, so a Date object is almost always serialized as an ISO string and must be explicitly parsed back on the other side.","Numeric map keys: JSON object keys are always strings, so a map keyed by integer ids becomes a map keyed by string ids after a round trip unless you convert it back.","Missing vs null vs undefined: many languages distinguish a field that is absent from one explicitly set to null, but JSON blurs this depending on the serializer used."]
items: Large integers: JSON numbers are represented as floating point, so integers beyond about 2^53 can lose precision silently during a round trip.
Dates: JSON has no native date type, so a Date object is almost always serialized as an ISO string and must be explicitly parsed back on the other side.
Numeric map keys: JSON object keys are always strings, so a map keyed by integer ids becomes a map keyed by string ids after a round trip unless you convert it back.
Missing vs null vs undefined: many languages distinguish a field that is absent from one explicitly set to null, but JSON blurs this depending on the serializer used.

blocks.title: A silent coercion bug
blocks.text: A client sends { "age": "30" } instead of { "age": 30 }. A loosely typed deserializer accepts it without complaint, and the string "30" flows all the way into a database column or a comparison like age > 18, which can behave correctly by accident or fail in ways that are hard to trace back to the original request.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pitfall","Typical Symptom"],"rows":[["Large integer precision loss","An id that is subtly wrong after a round trip through JSON"],["Unparsed date strings","Date comparisons failing silently because one side is a string and the other a real Date"],["Stringified numeric map keys","A lookup by numeric key failing after the data has passed through JSON once"],["Ambiguous null vs missing field","A field update handled differently than a field that was simply never sent"]]}

blocks.title: Schema binding is a contract, not a guarantee
blocks.content: A deserializer binding JSON onto a typed object is only as strict as you configure it to be. Many libraries coerce types quietly by default; a well designed API turns that off and rejects a mismatched type outright.
6. Common Formats and Their Tradeoffs

JSON, Protobuf, Avro, MessagePack, and XML are the formats you will meet most often, and this platform already has a dedicated Data Formats topic that compares them at a high level. What matters here is how each one approaches the actual mechanics of encoding and decoding, since that is what determines performance, schema strictness, and how forgiving a format is about change over time.

{"headers":["Format","Encoding","Schema","Typical Use"],"rows":[["JSON","Human readable text","None enforced by the format itself","Public APIs, browser to server traffic"],["Protobuf","Compact binary, field numbers","Required, defined in a .proto file","Service to service calls, gRPC"],["Avro","Compact binary, schema travels with data","Required, schema stored or attached","Data pipelines, Kafka messages"],["MessagePack","Compact binary, JSON like structure","None enforced","Fast drop in replacement for JSON"],["XML","Verbose, tag based text","Optional, via XSD","Legacy enterprise systems, SOAP"]]}

The pattern across the table is a genuine tradeoff, not a hierarchy. Text formats like JSON and XML are easy for a human to read in a log or a debugger, at the cost of larger payloads and slower parsing. Binary formats like Protobuf and Avro are smaller and faster to encode and decode, at the cost of needing extra tooling before a person can read them directly.
JSON

JSON encodes data as human readable text: braces for objects, brackets for arrays, quoted strings for text. Its biggest strength is universality, virtually every language and tool can read and write it without any extra setup, which is exactly why it dominates public APIs and browser facing traffic. Its biggest weakness is the loose type system covered in the previous section, which pushes correctness checking onto the application rather than the format.
Protobuf

Protocol Buffers require a schema written ahead of time in a .proto file, assigning every field a name and a numeric tag. Encoding skips field names entirely on the wire and writes only tag numbers and values in a compact binary layout, which is both smaller and faster to parse than JSON, at the cost of needing generated code and a shared schema file before anyone can read the bytes at all.
Avro

Avro takes schema seriously in a different way: the schema itself travels alongside the data, or is looked up from a shared schema registry, so a reader always knows exactly how to interpret the bytes even without a bundled generated class. This makes Avro a natural fit for data pipelines and Kafka topics, where producers and consumers are deployed independently and may run different code versions at the same time.
MessagePack

MessagePack keeps the same loose, schema free structure as JSON, objects, arrays, strings, numbers, but encodes it as compact binary instead of text. It is often described as a drop in replacement for JSON, useful when the format flexibility is still wanted but the size and parsing cost of plain text is not acceptable.
XML

XML predates JSON as the dominant text based interchange format and remains common in older enterprise systems and SOAP based APIs. Its tag based structure is more verbose than JSON, and it supports richer features such as namespaces and formal validation through XSD schemas, features that add real power at the cost of noticeably larger payloads and slower parsing.
7. Versioning and Backward Compatibility of Serialized Schemas
blocks.text: 7. Versioning and Backward Compatibility of Serialized Schemas

blocks.content: A schema almost never stays the same forever. Fields get added, fields get removed, and meanings shift as a product evolves. The hard part is that old serialized data, and old clients still running an older version of your schema, keep showing up long after the schema has moved on, so a deserializer has to cope with more than one version at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276115637-225607370.png
blocks.alt: Adding a new field is safe schema evolution, reusing an old field number or name breaks readers relying on the original schema

blocks.content: ["Additive changes are safe: adding a new optional field does not break readers that do not know about it yet.","Never reuse a field identifier: Protobuf field numbers and Avro field names, once shipped, should be retired, not recycled for a new meaning.","Give new fields sensible defaults: a reader on an old schema should degrade gracefully rather than crash when a field is missing.","Deprecate before removing: mark a field unused for a release or two before deleting it, so nothing depending on it breaks without warning."]
items: Additive changes are safe: adding a new optional field does not break readers that do not know about it yet.
Never reuse a field identifier: Protobuf field numbers and Avro field names, once shipped, should be retired, not recycled for a new meaning.
Give new fields sensible defaults: a reader on an old schema should degrade gracefully rather than crash when a field is missing.
Deprecate before removing: mark a field unused for a release or two before deleting it, so nothing depending on it breaks without warning.

blocks.title: Two directions of compatibility
blocks.content: Backward compatibility means new code can read old data. Forward compatibility means old code can read new data. A schema evolution strategy that only thinks about one direction eventually breaks the other.

blocks.title: A safe schema change in practice
blocks.text: A payments service adds an optional discountCode field to its event schema. Old consumers that have not been redeployed yet simply ignore the new field and keep working exactly as before, while newer consumers can start reading it immediately. Nothing had to be coordinated or deployed all at once.

blocks.content: 8. Deserialization Security Risks

Deserialization is not just a mechanical concern, it is also one of the more dangerous places in a backend if handled carelessly. Insecure deserialization is a recognised, OWASP class vulnerability where a deserializer is tricked, by a maliciously crafted payload, into constructing objects the developer never intended, sometimes leading all the way to remote code execution.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530154-4916713.png
blocks.alt: A deserializer that lets untrusted bytes choose their own class can be tricked into instantiating attacker-controlled code

blocks.content: The classic examples come from deserializers that are too powerful for their own good. Java ObjectInputStream, Python pickle, and PHP unserialize can all reconstruct arbitrary classes based purely on type information embedded in the payload itself. If an attacker controls that payload, they can potentially instruct the deserializer to instantiate classes with dangerous side effects in their constructors or property setters, all before your application code gets a chance to validate anything.

blocks.title: The rule that prevents most of these incidents
blocks.content: Never run a fully dynamic, type from payload deserializer on data that came from outside your system. Prefer formats and libraries that decode into a fixed, predeclared schema, such as JSON bound to a known class, and reject anything that does not match.
A deserializer is a program that runs on data you did not write. Treat every byte crossing that boundary as hostile until proven otherwise.
9. Performance Cost at Scale

Serialization and deserialization are not free. Every byte encoded and every byte decoded costs CPU time, and at low request volumes that cost is invisible. At the scale of millions of requests a day, it becomes a real line item, both in server CPU usage and in the network bandwidth spent moving larger payloads around.

{"headers":["Format","Relative Payload Size","Relative Encode/Decode Speed"],"rows":[["JSON","Larger, text based","Slower, needs character by character parsing"],["Protobuf","Small, binary, tagged","Fast, close to raw byte copies"],["MessagePack","Small, binary","Fast, comparable to Protobuf"],["XML","Largest, verbose tags","Slowest of the common formats"]]}

This is exactly why many companies keep JSON at the edge of their system, where readability and broad tooling support matter for public APIs and browser clients, while switching internal, service to service traffic to a binary format like Protobuf through gRPC. The public boundary optimizes for developer experience, and the internal boundary optimizes for raw throughput, and there is no contradiction in choosing differently for each.

blocks.title: Streaming avoids paying the full cost at once
blocks.content: Large payloads do not have to be fully deserialized into memory before use. Streaming parsers process a payload incrementally, keeping memory usage flat and letting processing start before the entire payload has even finished arriving.
10. Serialization for Caching and Storage

A cache like Redis has no concept of a JavaScript object or a Java class. It stores bytes and strings. Every time your application writes a computed value into the cache, that value has to be serialized first, and every time it reads that value back out, it has to be deserialized before your code can use it again.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530154-557466000.png
blocks.alt: A cache or database column only ever stores bytes, so every cached object is serialized going in and deserialized coming out

blocks.content: The same is true, in a slightly softer form, for many databases. Some modern databases store JSON natively as a first class column type, handling the encoding internally, while others expect you to serialize a complex object into a blob column yourself. Either way, the underlying mechanics described earlier in this topic, mapping, encoding, decoding, binding, are exactly what is happening under the hood, just triggered by a cache client or a database driver instead of an HTTP body parser.

blocks.title: Cache format choice matters more than it seems
blocks.content: A cache is usually read far more often than it is written. Choosing a fast to deserialize format for cached values, rather than the most compact one, often pays off more, since deserialization cost is paid on every cache hit.
11. Serialization for Inter Process Communication

When two processes need to exchange data, whether they sit on the same machine or across a network, they cannot share memory directly in the general case, so they fall back to the same serialize, transmit, deserialize pattern used everywhere else in this topic. A message queue serializes a message before placing it on the queue, and a consumer deserializes it after reading it off. A gRPC call serializes a request into a Protobuf message before sending it over the wire, and the receiving service deserializes it back into a usable object.

This is also where serialization quietly enables something bigger than any single request: cross language communication. A schema defined once, such as a .proto file, becomes a contract that a Java service and a Python service can both compile against, without either one knowing anything about the other internal object model. Neither side needs to understand the other language, only the shared, serialized shape of the data passing between them.
12. Common Pitfalls
A short list of mistakes accounts for most of the real world bugs and incidents tied to serialization.

["Losing precision on large numbers when round tripping through a text format like JSON.","Not handling deserialization failures gracefully, letting a malformed payload crash the process instead of returning a clean error.","Mismatched schema versions between a producer and a consumer that were deployed at different times.","Trusting deserialized data without validating it, which is exactly the gap the next topic in this series closes.","Non deterministic serialization, such as unordered object keys, which quietly breaks caching, hashing, or checksums that assume a stable byte representation."]
items: Losing precision on large numbers when round tripping through a text format like JSON.
Not handling deserialization failures gracefully, letting a malformed payload crash the process instead of returning a clean error.
Mismatched schema versions between a producer and a consumer that were deployed at different times.
Trusting deserialized data without validating it, which is exactly the gap the next topic in this series closes.
Non deterministic serialization, such as unordered object keys, which quietly breaks caching, hashing, or checksums that assume a stable byte representation.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pitfall","Typical Fix"],"rows":[["Precision loss on large numbers","Represent large ids as strings, or use a binary format with real integer types"],["Crash on malformed payload","Wrap deserialization in explicit error handling and return a clean 400 response"],["Producer and consumer schema drift","Version schemas explicitly and test compatibility before either side deploys"],["Unstable key ordering","Sort keys deterministically before hashing or checksumming a serialized payload"]]}

blocks.title: Deserialization is not the finish line
blocks.content: A successfully deserialized object is not the same thing as a correct one. It only means the bytes were structurally valid for the format. Whether the values inside make sense is a separate question, answered by validation, not deserialization.
13. Common Questions

Is JSON.stringify the same thing as encryption? No. Serialization makes data transmittable and readable in a standard format, it does nothing to hide it. Anyone who intercepts the bytes can read them exactly as easily as the intended recipient.

Why does my API return dates as strings? Because JSON has no native date type. The server serializes a Date object as an ISO 8601 string, and the client is responsible for parsing that string back into a real date value on its own side.

Why do some services use Protobuf instead of JSON internally? Because binary formats like Protobuf encode and decode faster and produce smaller payloads, which matters when a single request fans out into many internal service to service calls at scale.

What exactly makes deserialization insecure? A deserializer that reconstructs arbitrary object types based purely on information inside an untrusted payload, without validating what it is being asked to build, can be manipulated into constructing dangerous objects.

Does deserialization check whether the data is valid? No. It only checks whether the bytes are structurally well formed for the format. Checking whether the resulting values are actually correct is the job of the validation stage that runs immediately afterward.

How should a schema change without breaking existing clients? Favor additive, optional changes with sensible defaults, avoid reusing old field identifiers for new meanings, and deprecate fields for a release or two before removing them entirely.

Should I switch everything to a binary format for performance? Not by default. Reach for a binary format like Protobuf once you can point at an actual bottleneck, in payload size or CPU time, that JSON is causing. For most applications, JSON at the edge is a perfectly reasonable starting point.

Does compressing a payload replace the need to pick a good format? No. Compression, such as gzip, works alongside serialization, not instead of it. A verbose format compresses well but still costs real CPU time to encode, decode, and compress on both ends of the exchange.
14. Key Takeaways

["Serialization converts an in memory object into a portable form; deserialization reverses it.","Both exist because a process internal representation, full of pointers, cannot cross a network, disk, or process boundary on its own.","Serialization has two layers: mapping to a format representation, then encoding it into bytes; deserialization reverses both.","JSON type looseness causes real bugs: large number precision, date handling, and stringified numeric keys are common traps.","Insecure deserialization is a genuine, OWASP class security risk when a deserializer builds arbitrary types from untrusted input.","Binary formats like Protobuf and Avro trade human readability for smaller payloads and faster encode and decode at scale.","A successfully deserialized object is not a validated one; that check happens in the next stage of the pipeline.","Treat deserialization of untrusted input as running code on hostile data, and choose libraries and settings accordingly."]
items: Serialization converts an in memory object into a portable form; deserialization reverses it.
Both exist because a process internal representation, full of pointers, cannot cross a network, disk, or process boundary on its own.
Serialization has two layers: mapping to a format representation, then encoding it into bytes; deserialization reverses both.
JSON type looseness causes real bugs: large number precision, date handling, and stringified numeric keys are common traps.
Insecure deserialization is a genuine, OWASP class security risk when a deserializer builds arbitrary types from untrusted input.
Binary formats like Protobuf and Avro trade human readability for smaller payloads and faster encode and decode at scale.
A successfully deserialized object is not a validated one; that check happens in the next stage of the pipeline.
Treat deserialization of untrusted input as running code on hostile data, and choose libraries and settings accordingly.

blocks.content: Once a request body has been safely deserialized into a usable object, one question remains before any business logic should touch it: is this data actually correct, complete, and safe to act on. That question is answered by Request Validation and Transformation, the final stage in this three part journey through a request lifecycle.
